He followed this with their ugly deeds and their saying ﴿Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7], since they were the owners of wealth, while the Muhajirun were poor, having left their wealth and their trade and emigrated for the sake of Allah, the Exalted.

That is why it is followed by what follows an oath, and likewise the verb of certainty and knowledge functions like an oath, with His words ﴿that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah﴾. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra, as a verbal noun of *amana* (to believe). When He stated that they were liars, He followed it with the reason for their disbelief, which is that they took their oaths as a shield, by which they protected themselves and their wealth, as one poet said:

*They did not claim to be Muslim except to preserve their blood, lest they be shed.*

Al-Dahhak said: they took their oath by Allah that they were truly among you. Qatadah said: whenever something appeared from them that required their punishment, they swore falsely to protect their wealth and their blood. Al-Suddi said: "a shield" refers to abandoning the funeral prayer for them when they die. **﴿And they hinder﴾**, that is, they turned away and kept the Jews and the polytheists from entering Islam. **﴿That﴾**, that is, that false oath and that hindering, which made their deeds evil because of their faith and then their disbelief. Ibn Atiyyah said: "That" refers to Allah's act against them in exposing and rebuking them, and it may be that the reference is to the evil of what they did, so the meaning is: their deeds were evil in that they disbelieved. Al-Zamakhshari said: "That" refers to the statement that testifies against them that they are the worst of people in deeds, because they believed and then disbelieved; or it refers to what He described of their condition: hypocrisy, lying, and making light of faith. That is, all of that is because they believed and then disbelieved.

The majority read **﴿was set﴾** (*fa-tubi'a*) in the passive voice. Zayd ibn Ali read it in the active voice, meaning "Allah set," and likewise the reading of al-A'mash and Zayd in one narration, stating "Allah" explicitly. It is possible, according to Zayd's first reading, that the subject is a pronoun referring to the verbal noun implied by what precedes it, meaning "he set," that is, by their playing with religion. The meaning of **﴿they believed﴾** is that they uttered the testimony of faith and did what Muslims do. **﴿Then they disbelieved﴾** means their disbelief became apparent by what they uttered, such as their saying: "If what Muhammad says is true, then we are worse than donkeys," and their saying: "Does this man hope that the palaces of Kisra and Caesar will be opened to him? Far-fetched!" Or they uttered faith in the presence of the believers and disbelief in the presence of their devils. Or it refers to one who believed and then apostatized.

That is, because of their beauty, freshness, and loud voices, their appearance was pleasing and their speech was sweet. The majority read **﴿you listen﴾** with the second-person ta', while Ikrimah and Ata al-Awfi read *yusma'* with the ya' in the passive voice. Jarir said:

*You kept thinking every thing after them was horsemen charging against them, and men.*

He said: it is permissible that **﴿they are the enemy﴾** be the second object, just as if you omitted the pronoun. (If you ask): its proper form would be "she is the enemy." (I answer): it is considered with regard to the predicate, as is mentioned in "this is my Lord." It is also possible that a deleted noun is understood, so that the meaning is: "they think every person of the cry." End of quotation.

[p. 273] The reading of **"they are the enemy"** (al-Munafiqun: 4) as a second object of **yahsabuna** ("they think") is a forced construction, far from eloquence. What comes readily to a sound mind is that **"they are the enemy"** (al-Munafiqun: 4) is a report from Him, exalted is He, that they, even though they display Islam and their followers do so, are the ones most intent on enmity toward you. For this reason, after it comes His command, exalted is He, to beware of them, as He says: **"so beware of them"** (al-Munafiqun: 4). The command to beware is thus a consequence of His report that they are the enemy. **"May God destroy them"** (al-Munafiqun: 4) is a supplication that includes their distancing, and that the believers invoke this against them.

**"How are they turned away?"** (al-Munafiqun: 4), meaning: how are they diverted from the truth? It contains a note of wonder at their misguidance and ignorance. Since He, exalted is He, informed him of their enmity, He commanded him to beware of them, so he should not trust in their display of affection nor in the softness of their speech. **"May God destroy them"** (al-Munafiqun: 4) is a word of censure and reproach. The Arabs say, "May God destroy him, how perceptive he is!", using it in the place of wonder. Al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Raja', Ibn Abi Ishaq, Malik ibn Dinar, al-A'mash, Ibn Muhaysin, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Hasan al-'Anbari, and Abu 'Amr read **wa-akuna** ("and I would be") in the accusative, conjoined to **fa-assaddaqa**; likewise in the codices of 'Abd Allah and Ubayy. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read **wa-akunu** with **damma** on the **nun**, as a new sentence, meaning: "and I am going to be," and this is a promise of righteousness.

**"God will never delay a soul"** (al-Munafiqun: 11): In this is an exhortation to hasten to acts of obedience, for fear that the appointed term may come while one has neglected and not prepared for meeting God. The majority read **ta'malun** ("you do") with the second-person **ta'** addressed to all people. Abu Bakr read it with **ya'**, restricting the threat to the unbelievers, though the generality is possible.

[p. 273] The reading of **"they are the enemy"** (al-Munafiqun: 4) as a second object of **yahsabuna** ("they think") is a forced construction, far from eloquence. What comes readily to a sound mind is that **"they are the enemy"** (al-Munafiqun: 4) is a report from Him, exalted is He, that they, even though they display Islam and their followers do so, are the ones most intent on enmity toward you. For this reason, after it comes His command, exalted is He, to beware of them, as He says: **"so beware of them"** (al-Munafiqun: 4). The command to beware is thus a consequence of His report that they are the enemy. **"May God destroy them"** (al-Munafiqun: 4) is a supplication that includes their distancing, and that the believers invoke this against them.

**"How are they turned away?"** (al-Munafiqun: 4), meaning: how are they diverted from the truth? It contains a note of wonder at their misguidance and ignorance. Since He, exalted is He, informed him of their enmity, He commanded him to beware of them, so he should not trust in their display of affection nor in the softness of their speech. **"May God destroy them"** (al-Munafiqun: 4) is a word of censure and reproach. The Arabs say, "May God destroy him, how perceptive he is!", using it in the place of wonder. Whoever God destroys is vanquished, because He, exalted is He, is the Subduer of every obstinate one. **Kayfa** here is interrogative, meaning: how are they diverted from the truth while not seeing the right course of their own souls?

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is possible that **anna** ("how/whence") is an adverb of place governed by **qatalahum** ("may God destroy them"), as if he said: 'May God destroy them, how they turned away or were turned away.' In that case there is no interrogation in this statement." End of quote. But it is not valid for **anna** to be a mere adverb. It must be an interrogative adverb, either with the meaning of **ayna** ("where"), or **mata** ("when"), or **kayfa** ("how"), or a conditional with the meaning of **ayna**. In all these readings, what precedes it does not govern it, and it is never stripped of interrogative force to become a general adverb of place without the consideration we have mentioned. So the view that it is such is invalid.

When God vindicated Zayd ibn Arqam regarding what he reported about Ibn Salul, the people despised Ibn Salul, and the believers of his own people blamed him. Some of them said to him: "Go to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), confess your sin, and he will ask forgiveness for you." He turned his head away, rejecting this opinion, and said to them: "You advised me to believe, so I believed; you advised me to give the zakat of my wealth, so I gave it. Nothing remains for you except that you order me to prostrate to Muhammad." **Yastaghfir** ("he will ask forgiveness") is jussive, in response to the imperative. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) requires two governing verbs: one is **yastaghfir** and the other is **ta'alaw** ("come"). He made the second govern, according to the preferred view of the Basrans. If he had made the first govern, the construction would have been: "Come, you will be forgiven by the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

Mujahid, Nafi', the people of Medina, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, al-Mufaddal, Aban on the authority of 'Asim, al-Hasan, and Ya'qub, with a variant from the two of them, read **lawwaw** with the **waw** unstressed. Abu Ja'far, al-A'mash, Talhah, 'Isa, Abu Raja', al-A'raj, and the rest of the Seven read it with the **waw** stressed, for intensity. **Lawaw ru'usahum** ("they turned their heads") is by way of mockery. The Messenger's asking forgiveness for them is his calling them to repent from hypocrisy; he asks forgiveness for them because his asking forgiveness is a consequence of their repentance. But they turn away, avoiding the coming and the Messenger's asking forgiveness. It is also read **yasuddun** ("they turn away"), and **yasuddun** is a circumstantial clause (hal). The present tense is used to show their persistence. **Wa hum mustakbirun** ("while they are arrogant") is also a circumstantial clause.

Since it had already been decided in His knowledge, exalted is He, that they would never believe, He made equal for them His asking forgiveness and its absence. Makki reported that he, peace be upon him, had asked forgiveness for them, because they had displayed Islam to him. Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse was revealed after His saying, exalted is He, in Bara'ah: **"Even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times"** (al-Tawbah: 80), and after his saying, peace be upon him: "I will ask forgiveness for them more than seventy times." Then this verse was revealed, and so there was no longer any basis for asking forgiveness.

The majority read **astaghfarta** with the **hamzat al-taswiyah** ("equalizing hamza"), whose origin is the interrogative hamza, and the **alif al-wasl** ("connecting alif") is dropped. Abu Ja'far read it with a long vowel on the hamza. It was said: this is a substitute for the connecting hamza, and it is like the long vowel in His saying: **"Say: has He forbidden the two males"** (al-An'am: 143). But this long vowel is in the noun, so that the interrogative is not confused with the declarative, whereas this is not needed in the verb, because the connecting hamza in the verb is kasra-vowelled. It is also reported from Abu Ja'far: the **damma** on the **mim** of **'alayhim** ("upon them") because its origin is **damma**, with the hamza connected. Mu'adh ibn Mu'adh al-'Anbari reported from Abu 'Amr the **kasra** on the **mim** according to the original rule for meeting of two quiescent letters, with the hamza connected, so that it drops in both readings. The wording is declarative, but the meaning is interrogative, and the intention is equalizing. The hamza may be dropped because **am** ("or") indicates it, just as it indicates its dropping in the poet's line:

"With seven we threw the pebbles, or with eight?"

meaning: "Was it with seven?" Al-Zamakhshari said: Abu Ja'far read **a-staghfarta**, prolonging the interrogative hamza for clarity and explanation, not converting the connecting hamza into an alif as in **a-l-siHr** ("the magic") and **a-llah** ("God"). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read **a-staghfarta** with a long vowel on the hamza, which is the alif of equalizing. And he read also with connecting the alif without hamza, as a declarative. But in all of this there is weakness: in the first he kept the connecting hamza although the interrogative hamza has already made it unnecessary; and in the second he dropped the interrogative hamza although he intends it, and this is something used only in poetry.

**"They are the ones who say"** (al-Munafiqun: 7) refers to Ibn Salul and those of his people who agreed with him. It mocks their folly in thinking that the provision of the emigrants was in their hands, though they did not know that this was in the hand of God, exalted is He.

**"Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God"** (al-Munafiqun: 7): If God, exalted is He, is relating the exact words of their speech, then their saying **"those who are with the Messenger of God"** is by way of mockery, like their saying: **"They say, 'O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are truly mad'"** (al-Hijr: 6). Or because it had become, in their view, like a game: meaning, he is known by the application of this term to him. For had they been affirming his messengerhood, what they did would not have come from them. The apparent meaning is that they did not utter this exact wording; rather, God, exalted is He, expressed by it His Messenger (ﷺ), honoring and exalting him.

The majority read **yanfaddu** ("they scatter"), meaning: they disperse from the Messenger. Al-Fadl ibn 'Isa read **yanfadduu** from **infadda al-qawm** ("the people ran out of food"): when their food ran out, the man shook out his bag. The verb is of the type that is transitive without the **hamza**, and with the **hamza** it is not transitive. Al-Zamakhshari said: its real sense is that the time has come for them to shake out their saddlebags.

The majority read **"The mightier will surely expel the weaker from it"** (al-Munafiqun: 8). Here **al-a'azz** is the subject and **al-adhall** is the object, and this is from the speech of Ibn Salul, as mentioned earlier. By "the mightier" he means himself and his companions, and by "the weaker" the believers. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and al-Musayyabi in his choice read **la-nukhrijanna** with the **nun**, and they put **al-a'azz** and **al-adhall** in the accusative: **al-a'azz** is the object, and **al-adhall** is a circumstantial state (hal). Al-Hasan read, as Abu 'Amr al-Dani reported, **la-nakhrujanna** with the **nun** of plurality vowelled with **fatha** and the **ra'** with **damma**, and with **al-a'azz** in the accusative as a specification, like the saying: "We Arabs are the most generous of people to guests"; and with **al-adhall** in the accusative as a state. Abu Hatim also reported this reading. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' reported that some people read **la-yakhrujanna** with the **ya'** vowelled with **fatha** and the **ra'** with **damma**, so the subject is **al-a'azz**, and **al-adhall** is in the accusative as a state. It is also read in the passive with **ya'**: **al-a'azz** is raised by it, and **al-adhall** is in the accusative as a state.

The coming of a state (hal) in the form of a definite noun is interpreted by the Basran grammarians as an extra use of the definite article, not that it is definite. Where it has **al-**, it is considered to be an added article, not a true definite.

When 'Abd Allah, son of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, heard this verse, he came to his father and said: "By God, father, you are the weak one, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is the mighty one." When he approached Medina, he drew his sword against him and prevented him from entering until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave him permission. Among what he said to him was: "Stay back; you will not enter it until you say: 'The Messenger of God (ﷺ) is the mighty, and I am the weak.'" He remained held in his hand until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave permission for him to be released. In this report, he said to his father: "If you do not testify that might belongs to God and His Messenger, I will surely strike off your neck." He said: "Would you really do it?" He said: "Yes." So he said: "I testify that might belongs to God, to His Messenger, and to the believers."

It was said to al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with both of them: "There is arrogance in you." He said: "It is not arrogance, but dignity," and he recited this verse.

**"Let neither your wealth"** (al-Munafiqun: 9) diverts you through striving for its increase and delighting in gathering it; **"nor your children"** through your joy in them and looking after their welfare, in your lifetime and after your death; **"from the remembrance of God"** (al-Munafiqun: 9). This is general, including the prayer, and praising God, exalted is He, with glorification, praise, and other things, and supplication. Al-Hasan and a group said something similar. Al-Dahhak and 'Ata' said: here it specifically emphasizes the obligatory prayer. Al-Hasan also said: all the obligations. Al-Kalbi said: jihad alongside the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It was also said: the Qur'an.

**"Whoever does that"** (al-Munafiqun: 9), that is, the preoccupation away from the remembrance of God through wealth and children, **"those are the losers"** (al-Munafiqun: 9), because they preferred the hasty over the deferred, and the perishing over the enduring.

**"Spend from what We have provided you"** (al-Munafiqun: 10). The majority said: what is meant is zakat. It was also said: it is general, including the obligatory and the recommended. From Ibn 'Abbas: it was revealed concerning those who withheld zakat. "By God, if he saw good, he would not ask for return." It was said to him: "Do you not fear God? The believers ask for a return." He said: "Yes, I recite to you a Qur'an about it," meaning that it was revealed concerning the believers, and they are the ones addressed by it.

**"Why did You not delay me"** (al-Munafiqun: 10), that is: would that You had delayed my death to a short time? The majority read **fa-assaddaqa** ("so I would give charity"), which is in the accusative as an answer to the wish. Ubayy, 'Abd Allah, and Ibn Jubayr read **fa-atasaddaqa** according to the original form. The majority of the Seven read **wa-akun** ("and I would be") as jussive. Al-Zamakhshari said: **wa-akun** in the jussive is a conjunction with the position of **fa-assaddaqa**, as if it were said: "If You delay me, I will give charity and be." End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: a conjunction with the position, since the sense is: "If You delay me, I will give charity and be." This is the view of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. As for what Sibawayh reported from al-Khalil, it is other than this: he made **wa-akun** jussive by treating as if there were a conditional, implied by the wish, and there is no position here, because the conditional is not apparent; a conjunction with the position is made only where the conditional appears, as in His saying, exalted is He: **"Whomever God leaves astray, there is no guide for him, and He leaves them"** (al-A'raf: 186). Whoever reads with the jussive conjoins to the position of **"there is no guide for him"** (al-A'raf: 186), because if a verb occurred there it would be jussive. End of quote.
